name: Ceftazidime
route_note: IV or IM injection every 8 hours; also combined with avibactam.

discovery.note: Developed around 1980; a carboxypropyl-oxyimino side chain and pyridinium group give strong activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

tagline: Anti-pseudomonal cephalosporin used for melioidosis, neutropenic fever and HAP
summary: Ceftazidime is a third-generation cephalosporin with strong activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa but weak Gram-positive activity. It is used for serious hospital infections, febrile neutropenia and melioidosis, and is the partner drug in ceftazidime-avibactam.
mechanism: Ceftazidime binds primarily PBP3 of Gram-negative bacilli, blocking septum formation and cell-wall synthesis, which leads to filamentation and lysis.
It is stable to many plasmid beta-lactamases but is hydrolysed by ESBLs, derepressed AmpC and carbapenemases; adding avibactam restores activity against many class A, C and some class D enzymes.

history.title: Introduction
history.detail: Ceftazidime enters clinical use in the early 1980s (Fortum/Fortaz).

history.title: Melioidosis trial
history.detail: A Thai randomised trial shows ceftazidime halves mortality of severe melioidosis compared with conventional therapy.

history.title: EU approval of combination
history.detail: Ceftazidime-avibactam (Zavicefta) is authorised in the European Union.

history.title: WHO AWaRe classification
history.detail: The WHO Essential Medicines List begins grouping antibiotics into Access, Watch and Reserve categories; ceftazidime is placed in the Watch group.

serious: Neurotoxicity (encephalopathy, seizures) with accumulation in renal impairment

facts: Ceftazidime is one of the few cephalosporins recommended for intensive-phase treatment of melioidosis.
It is classified in the WHO 'Watch' antibiotic group.
